EUCOM Europe’s geography and geopolitical landscape make certain risks more pronounced than others. Europe is adopting advanced energy technologies at a higher rate compared to other continents (see Figure D-1), with nearly half of the European Union’s (E.U.’s) electricity now generated from advanced energy technologies such as wind, solar, hydropower, bioenergy, geothermal, and ocean energy technologies (Eurostat 2025b). The continent lacks significant domestic reserves of legacy fuels, such as oil and natural gas, making Europe heavily reliant on foreign energy suppliers. The unique nature of Europe’s economic and political integration through institutions such as the E.U. and NATO creates a more interconnected energy ecosystem, resulting in opportunities and risks shared across borders. This has implications for European resilience and U.S. military operations in the U.S. European Command (EUCOM) theater. Figure D-1. Source: IEA 2024d D.1 Strategic Leadership The changing global energy landscape is reshaping the foundation of geopolitical influence, with advanced energy systems increasingly viewed not only as alternative forms of energy but also as instruments of power projection and strategic alignment. In the European theater, as legacy fuel markets shrink and nations accelerate their shift toward advanced energy technologies, a new set of dependencies is emerging. Although Europe has made significant progress in reducing its reliance on fossil fuels from Russia and the Middle East, the continent now faces increasing exposure to another form of strategic vulnerability: dependence on China for critical materials, technologies, and manufacturing supply chains that underpin the adoption of advanced energy technologies. China’s control of installed components creates cyber vulnerabilities (CISA 2022), and an embargo of inputs to advanced energy assets could degrade Europe’s grid and undermine economic growth. While China may not currently use this dependence to overtly coerce European actors, the deep integration of Chinese materials and technologies into Europe’s energy ecosystem creates a latent influence that can shape European policy decisions over time, 67 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. encouraging European decision makers to carefully weigh the risks of antagonizing China on unrelated geopolitical issues. Dependence on Chinese manufacturing could also hinder Europe’s technological development and defense readiness in the future.
